t: LeetCode 466 — Count The Repetitions: Cycle Detection on Subsequence Matching
o: We must find the maximum m such that s2 repeated n2*m times is a subsequence of s1 repeated n1 times. Equivalently, count how many full copies of s2 can be matched while scanning str1, then divide by n2. Since n1 and n2 can be up to 10^6 and strings up to length 100, brute force over all characters of str1 (up to 10^8) is borderline but the smarter approach exploits structure: as we consume copies of s1, the state is just the index j into s2 where we start. There are at most len(s2) distinct states, so within len(s2)+1 consumed copies of s1 a state must repeat, giving a cycle we can jump over. In example 1, scanning "acb" four times matches "ab" twice total, so [s2,2] fits once → answer 2.
k: The only state that matters when consuming one copy of s1 is the position j in s2 where matching begins; everything else is determined by it.
With at most len(s2) ≤ 100 distinct states, a repeat of (j) after consuming some number of s1-copies is guaranteed quickly, enabling cycle detection and huge jumps.
Track counts of completed s2 per s1-copy consumed; use the pre-cycle prefix plus (full cycles) + remainder to get totals without simulating all n1 copies.

a.i: Simply scan through each of the n1 copies of s1 character by character, advancing a pointer into s2 whenever characters match, and counting how many times s2 completes. This directly models the subsequence-matching process. With n1 up to 10^6 and |s1| up to 100 this is up to 10^8 operations — often accepted in practice due to early exits, but not asymptotically optimal.
s: Initialize index j = 0 into s2 and counter cnt = 0 for completed s2 copies.
For each of the n1 copies of s1, iterate over its characters c.
If c == s2[j], increment j; if j reaches len(s2), increment cnt and reset j = 0.
a.t: O(n1 * |s1|) time — we scan every character of str1 once.
a.sp: O(1) extra space — only pointers and counters.

a.n: Approach 2: Cycle Detection on Match-Start Index (Optimal)
a.i: Record, for each starting index j in s2, how many s2-copies complete and what j becomes after consuming exactly one copy of s1. Since there are at most |s2| possible values of j, within |s2|+1 iterations a state repeats, forming a cycle. Split the n1 copies into a prefix before the cycle, k full cycles, and a tail, computing the total s2-count in O(1) per part instead of iterating all n1 copies.
s: Iterate i from 1 to n1, consuming one copy of s1 starting from current index j; record cnt[i] (cumulative s2 completions) and nextIndex[i] = resulting j.
If j was seen before at iteration p, we found a cycle: patternLen = i - p, patternCount = cnt[i] - cnt[p].
Compute total = cnt[p] + patternCount * ((n1 - p) / patternLen) + (cnt[p + (n1 - p) % patternLen] - cnt[p]).
a.t: O(|s2| * |s1|) time — the loop runs at most |s2|+1 iterations before a cycle is found, each costing O(|s1|).
a.sp: O(|s2|) space for the recorded indices and cumulative counts.

w: In an interview, mention the direct simulation first to show you understand the subsequence process, then immediately propose cycle detection since n1 up to 10^6 makes pure simulation risky. Common pitfalls: forgetting that a partial match of s2 still consumes part of an s1 copy (the state j carries across copies), off-by-one errors in the cycle arithmetic (prefix length p vs. cycle start), and integer overflow of counts in C++/Java (use long). Edge cases: s2 containing letters absent from s1 (answer 0), n1 smaller than the cycle length (loop naturally terminates without finding a cycle), and s2 of length 1. Follow-ups may ask to return the actual matched string length or handle streaming input where n1 is unknown.
